text:
Two separate changes that everyone keeps saying as one sentence, so writing them down apart.

One: the version. 14 to 17, pg_upgrade --link, about four minutes of read-only. Boring, and I want it to stay boring.

Two: the pooler. We hold 1,180 backend connections at peak against max_connections 1500, and roughly 900 of those are idle at any moment. Four scheduler replicas, the api, the runner claim path and the reporting user. pgbouncer in transaction mode takes that to under a hundred server connections.

The version is a date in a calendar. The pooler is a behaviour change and it needs a list. I want every place we depend on something surviving between two statements, in this thread, before Tuesday.

Filing this rather than leaving it in my head.

We keep audit log rows forever because nobody has ever decided otherwise. The control we have written says retained for a defined period with documented access, and defined period is currently a lie - it is not defined, it is unbounded because deleting is work.

Two decisions are needed and neither is technical. How long do we keep entries, and who inside Kiln may read them. The auditor will ask for the second one with names, and the honest answer today is anyone with production database access.

conversation.name: Per-org concurrency contracts

title: Per-org concurrency contracts
text:
Closes #375. Behind concurrency.contracts, default off.

Contracts live in the same migration as the share weights: guaranteed, ceiling, depth_cap per org, with the plan default written as a real row rather than left null. Dispatch counts live leases for the org, compares against the contract and either places or skips. The count and the lease insert happen in one transaction with the org's contract row locked, so two dispatchers cannot both read nine of ten.

The ceiling only applies while the fleet is under 70% utilised. Above that everyone is held to their guarantee, which is the number we promised and the only one we can keep when the fleet is full.

This is #310 again with a different noun. In March we decided whose job runs next and left how many alone, and #310's own ADR says placement is not admission - I wrote that sentence and then spent three months not reading it.

Soak is 4,200 jobs from one org at t=0 against forty orgs trickling. Old path: the trickle's p95 wait is 6m40s. Contracts on: 52s, and the big org finishes eleven minutes later than it would have, which is the trade and it should be said plainly.

text:
The bake has been running nightly since last Tuesday and staging has been on it since Friday. This is the part that puts it in front of real builds.

On boot the runner reads the manifest, resolves the tag to a digest, and refuses to start if the digest it booted with is not the digest the manifest names. If the manifest is unreadable, unsigned or older than the maximum age it takes the cold start path instead of guessing. Cold start still works and is still tested; it is the fallback now rather than the norm.

We fixed who goes next in March. We never fixed how many an org can be running at once. Concurrency is still a number attached to the plan, so every org on enterprise shares one limit and the first one to fill it holds it.

On the night of the 16th Northwind had about 340 builds running against an enterprise limit of 400. That is not a bug in the limiter. The limiter did exactly what it says. It is that the number it enforces is not a promise to anybody - not to Northwind, who cannot plan against it, and not to the four orgs who were behind them.

text:
Tracking issue for the metering rewrite. I am going to spend this week reading before I write anything, because the thing I keep tripping over is that there is no single answer to what a build minute is.

Three paths compute it. The usage API sums build durations from the raw rows. The invoice renderer sums the daily rollup. The dashboard calls the API but caches for an hour, so it is the API with a different clock.

Two of those round, at different points, for different reasons. Neither is wrong on its own terms. Together they are three numbers with one name, and support has to say which one the customer is looking at before they can answer anything.

Their external auditor reconciles our invoice against our usage API every month. Five months, five mismatches, always the same direction:

March invoice GBP 9,412.03, API 9,412.05
April GBP 8,977.44, API 8,977.47
May GBP 10,204.18, API 10,204.21
June GBP 9,860.77, API 9,860.79
July GBP 11,006.52, API 11,006.56

Fourteen pence in total. They are not asking for the money. They are asking which of the two numbers is the one we stand behind, in writing, because their auditor will not sign off a supplier whose own two systems disagree.

text:
From this morning's retro. Five items, an owner on each, and the dates are the owner's own.

1. Alert when dispatch has been zero for 90 seconds, and make a no-data result page rather than resolve. Wren. This week.

2. One lock order everywhere: the contract row before any lease row, with a test that fails if either path changes. Marin. This week, #416.

3. Remove contracts.checkOnRenewal once item 2 is in production, and count how often admission and renewal want the same row so we know whether the contention is real. Marin. This week.

4. A runbook entry for the queue has stopped dispatching, including how to read pg_locks and what a livelock looks like against a deadlock. Rafael Pinto. End of the month.

5. A soak in CI that runs admission and renewal together at contract limits for 60 orgs. Marin. No date, which is honest rather than good.

Idle is reported by the runner heartbeat, which is every 30 seconds. A 120 second window gives you four samples per machine and the heartbeat is best-effort - we drop them under load. Does the alert fire when the fleet is busy enough to lose heartbeats, which is the moment you least want a false page?

conversation.name: Scheduler stopped dispatching between 21:30 and 23:30 on 11 August

title: Scheduler stopped dispatching between 21:30 and 23:30 on 11 August
text:
Timeline, before anyone reconstructs it from memory.

21:30 - the contract sync starts its first busy run. It takes a row lock on every contract and holds them.
21:31 - renewal transactions begin blocking on those rows. They are already holding lease rows.
21:33 - dispatch blocks on the same contract rows. Postgres kills one side of each cycle, the dispatcher retries, and the retry deadlocks again. From here the queue is stopped.
22:10 - first page. Depth took forty minutes to cross 2,000 because it is a Tuesday in August.
22:14 - bridge. 22:47 - cause.
23:02 - sync disabled. 23:30 - dispatch back.
23:40 - renewal stops reading the contract row.
00:15 - closed.

The part I want read is not the fix. Bruno wrote this exact failure into the review of #376 on 25 June - lease renewal writes the same rows and does not take the contract lock, fine until something needs to. I replied that it was fine. It was fine for seven weeks.

Closes kiln/runner#208.

Each runner in the pool carries its own idle clock. A runner idle for 120 seconds is released, unless releasing it would take the pool below its floor. Releases go one at a time with 30 seconds between them, so a quiet minute does not drain the pool and make the next burst pay for it.

The clock being per runner rather than per pool is the actual bug. The pool-level clock was reset by activity anywhere in the pool, so a trickle held every machine.

warm_test drives one claim every 40 seconds for 30 simulated minutes and asserts the pool is back at its floor. No sleeps - the clock is an interface.

conversation.name: ADR-0026: prebaked images replace the warm pool

title: ADR-0026: prebaked images replace the warm pool
text:
This supersedes ADR-0022, which I wrote in May.

ADR-0022 argued that a warm pool beats prebaked images because the pool is live in a day and an image takes twenty minutes to bake. I was right about the timeline and wrong about the price. Sixteen machines resident across four availability zones is 7,030 EUR a month, against the 2,050 the ADR estimated, because the estimate assumed the pool drains during the day and it does not - the refill loop keeps it full at three in the morning.

What replaces it: one base image per region with the three common toolchains resident, baked nightly from a manifest, and the ASG launch template reading the image id. Cold start should land between 10 and 13 seconds against 9.4 with the pool and 38.1 with neither.

It is worse than the pool and about a tenth of the cost. That is the whole decision.

title: Scheduler stopped dispatching between 21:30 and 23:30 on 11 August
text:
pg_stat_activity is 190 rows of dispatch transactions in `Lock` wait, and the log has this every second or so:

`ERROR: deadlock detected. Process 18422 waits for ShareLock on transaction 9814022; blocked by process 18901.`

The cycle is contracts against leases. Dispatch locks the org's contract row and then inserts a lease. Renewal updates the lease rows and then reads the contract row FOR SHARE - it has done that since July. Those two orders are opposite and they have never both been busy at the same time until tonight.

conversation.name: Per-org concurrency contracts: enforce the limit at dispatch

title: Per-org concurrency contracts: enforce the limit at dispatch
text:
The contract table landed last week. This is the part that uses it.

Dispatch reads the org's current count before it places, and skips the org when it is at its contract rather than rejecting the job. A skipped org keeps its deficit, so it is picked first the moment a slot frees - being at your limit should cost you nothing once you are under it again.

conversation.name: A cancelled build releases its lease instead of waiting for it to expire

title: A cancelled build releases its lease instead of waiting for it to expire
text:
Found this reading concurrency.ts on Tuesday. Cancelling a build marks it cancelled and tells the runner to stop. The lease row stays until its expiry, which is thirty seconds away.

For thirty seconds the org is counted as holding a machine it is not holding. An org sitting at its contract limit that cancels five builds waits half a minute before it can submit anything, and the message it gets says it is at its limit, which is not true.

Release on cancel, and the release is idempotent so a runner reporting the same cancel twice is not a problem.

conversation.name: Enforce the org's limit at lease renewal, not only at dispatch

title: Enforce the org's limit at lease renewal, not only at dispatch
text:
Admission checks the limit when a build starts and never again. If support lowers a contract while builds are running - which is the only time anyone lowers one - the org stays over its number until every running job finishes, and on a monorepo that is an hour.

Renewal now re-reads the contract and the org's live lease count in the same transaction as the extension, and refuses the renewal if the org is over. A refused renewal requeues the job at the head of that org's queue rather than failing the build, and it carries limit_source from #386 so support sees the same word they see on a 409.

Soak is 200 orgs with contracts lowered under load. No requeue storm, p95 wait unchanged at 41s.

conversation.name: Claim honours Retry-After and stops retrying in lockstep

title: Claim honours Retry-After and stops retrying in lockstep
text:
Action item two from the 0078 retro, and the cheapest of the five.

On a 429 the claim loop currently waits a fixed two seconds and tries again. Every runner that got a 429 in the same second retries in the same second, forever, which is how a rate limit becomes a load test.

Now it reads Retry-After when the server sends one, falls back to exponential backoff when it does not, caps at sixty seconds, and jitters by up to a quarter of the interval. The header does not exist yet - Marin is adding it to the limiter today - so for now this is the fallback path and by tomorrow it is not.

conversation.name: Per-org concurrency contracts

title: Per-org concurrency contracts
text:
The index on (org, expires_at) is in the migration, good. Two things about the lock.

You take it on the contract row for the whole transaction, and the transaction also inserts a lease. Lease renewal writes the same lease rows and does not take the contract lock. Today that is fine because renewal never touches contracts. It is fine until something needs to.

Also: contracts change rarely, so the row is almost never contended and the lock is almost always free, which means if this is ever wrong it will be wrong at the worst possible moment and never in a test.

conversation.name: Postgres 17: what has to be true before we cut over

title: Postgres 17: what has to be true before we cut over
text:
We are on 14.12. 14 goes out of support in November 2026, so this is a thing we have to do rather than a thing we would like to do. The primary is 1.4 TB and everything except the audit log is hot.

What I want out of this issue is the list of things that have to be true before a cutover, not a date. My starting four:

1. Connection count. Four scheduler replicas, the API, the runner claim path and two reporting users add up to about 340 connections against max_connections 400. That is the number that decides whether pgbouncer is part of this or a separate project.
2. Logical replication from 14 to 17 for the cutover, which means every table needs a primary key and two of them do not.
3. The claim path uses SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED at a rate nothing else in the system comes close to, and I would like a number for it on 17 before I trust one.
4. Rollback. Once we are writing to 17 there is no going back without losing writes, so the plan has to say what we do instead.

The packing is not the thing I want to talk about. The packing is right.

conversation.name: Bill build minutes in the org's currency, and round once

title: Bill build minutes in the org's currency, and round once
text:
The last piece of the metering rewrite, and the one that matters to a customer.

Today: each build's duration is rounded to two decimal places in EUR, converted to the org's currency at that moment, and the rounded converted figures are summed. Three roundings per build, and the error is systematic rather than random because the conversion always rounds the same way.

After: durations are summed as whole seconds, the total is priced in EUR as an integer number of cents, converted once at the rate for the invoice date, and rounded once at the end. On Northwind's August invoice that is 18,412.60 GBP against 18,408.35, so we have been under-billing them by 4.25 - which is not the direction anyone expected.

conversation.name: ADR-0025: per-org concurrency contracts

title: ADR-0025: per-org concurrency contracts
text:
Four sections, and it rewrites the fair-share concept page rather than sitting beside it, because these are the same decision made twice.

One: what happened on 16 June, in numbers. Two: why the fair queue did not prevent it - it decides who goes next and says nothing about how many you may be running. Three: the contract. A guaranteed concurrency an org can plan against, a ceiling it may reach while the fleet is below 70% utilised, and a queue depth cap above which submission is refused with a Retry-After. Four: what this is not.

The part I am least sure of is the ceiling being conditional on fleet utilisation. It means an org's throughput depends on what other orgs are doing, which is exactly the property we removed in March. I think it is right because the alternative is idle machines, but it is the sentence to argue with.

title: Plan limit becomes a floor that scales with seats
text:
Closes #391.

An org with no contract gets the plan limit plus one per ten seats, rounded down, capped at its fair share of the fleet. Standard stays a floor of 12, so nobody goes backwards, and a sixty seat org on standard gets 18 instead of 12.

The cap matters more than the increase. Without it a big enough org on a small plan can quietly become the whole queue, which is the thing ADR-0025 exists to stop.

limit_source stays plan for these, because from support's point of view it is still the plan deciding.

conversation.name: Cold start: warm pool, prebaked images, or a smaller base

title: Cold start: warm pool, prebaked images, or a smaller base
text:
Three ways to not pay 38 seconds. Writing them down so we argue about the same things.

1. Warm pool. Keep n idle runners booted with the image already pulled. Cold start goes to roughly the handshake, so about 3s. Costs whatever n idle machines cost, all the time.

2. Prebaked images. Bake the toolchain into the AMI so the pull is a local read. Cold start maybe 10s. Costs a bake pipeline and a delay between pushing a toolchain change and it being available.

3. Smaller base image. 41 layers to about 12, drop the build-essential set. Cold start maybe 24s. Cheapest, smallest win, and we would still be here in September.

I want 1. I am aware I want 1 partly because I could have it running on Friday.

conversation.name: Postgres 17 and a pooler: the list of things that break

title: Postgres 17 and a pooler: the list of things that break
text:
Scheduler, four:

1. lease.ts takes pg_advisory_lock on the org id and releases it at the end of the renewal. Session-scoped. Under transaction pooling that lock is held on whichever server connection we happened to get and nothing ever releases it.
2. Named prepared statements, cached per client connection by the driver.
3. fairshare.ts builds the share snapshot as a temp table and placement.ts joins against it in a second statement.
4. The queue wakeup is LISTEN/NOTIFY.

1 and 2 have known answers. 4 needs its own pool. 3 is the one I have no clean answer for yet.

conversation.name: Alert when the share table has been stale for more than 90 seconds

title: Alert when the share table has been stale for more than 90 seconds
text:
The last thing on the ADR-0021 list. The gauge went in last week; this is the alert that reads it.

Refresh is every 15s. The alert fires when the table has been older than 90s continuously for five minutes, which is six missed refreshes and cannot be a single slow one. There is also a counter for placements that took the FIFO fallback, so the ratio is visible without a page.

The point of this is that the fallback is safe and invisible, and invisible is how we end up running the old queue in June and presenting a graph about the new one.

conversation.name: Count an org's live leases once per tick, not once per candidate

title: Count an org's live leases once per tick, not once per candidate
text:
Since the concurrency contracts went in, dispatch asks the database how many leases an org holds before it will place anything for that org. One query per candidate org per tick. At sixty queued orgs and a two second tick that is thirty queries a second whose answer barely changes.

One grouped query per tick now, held as a snapshot for the duration of the tick. Dispatch reads the snapshot. If the snapshot is older than one tick it is not used and we fall back to the per-org query, so the worst case of this change is the behaviour we have today.

Soak over two hours with ninety orgs, half of them sitting at their contract limit: p95 queue wait 41s before, 38s after, and the scheduler's database time drops from 22% of the tick to under 3%.

From this morning. Three gaps, and the auditor will test all three.

One: we record writes and not reads. A control that says you can detect unauthorised access to customer data cannot be evidenced by a log that only knows about changes.

Two: there is no retention policy. The table has never been pruned and there is no archive, so the honest answer to how long we keep it is until somebody runs out of disk.

Three: anyone with production database access can read it and nothing records that they did. That is the same twelve accounts from the March access review.

One of these is a week of work and two of them are a decision nobody has made.

conversation.name: ADR-0027: audit log retention and access

title: ADR-0027: audit log retention and access
text:
Three sections: what we keep today and for how long, who can read it today, and what changes.

The proposal is 400 days. Thirteen months plus five weeks, so an annual audit can always look back a full year including the month it is happening in. Reads become a role on the org membership rather than a property of being an owner, and Kiln-side access becomes an explicit grant that expires.

The part I want argued with is that deleting is irreversible and an auditor can read 'we delete evidence on a schedule' as a finding. The counter-argument is that keeping everything forever is also a finding, and a worse one, because it means nobody decided. I believe the counter-argument and I am not certain of it.

title: Count an org's live leases at dispatch, not this replica's counter
text:
Closes #381.

The in-memory counter is gone. Placement does a conditional insert against the lease table - `insert ... select where (select count(*) from leases where org = $1 and expires_at > now()) < $2` - so the count and the claim are one statement and four replicas cannot each spend the same slot.

The expiry filter is the part worth reading. Counting rows that exist rather than rows that are live means a crashed runner holds a slot until the reaper deletes it, and the reaper is a minute behind on a bad day.

conversation.name: Shed an org that is ignoring 429s before the limiter costs anything

title: Shed an org that is ignoring 429s before the limiter costs anything
text:
From last night.

The limiter is correct and it is expensive. Every refusal reads a Redis counter and resolves the org in Postgres, so a client that retries into a closed door consumes the same backend work as one that is being served.

This counts consecutive 429s per org in process memory. Twenty in a sixty second window and that org gets a static 429 with Retry-After for the next thirty seconds, answered from the edge, touching nothing. The counter is reset by one successful request.

It is deliberately not exact. Four api replicas each keep their own count, so the real threshold is somewhere between twenty and eighty depending on how the load balancer feels. That is fine: the thing this protects against is four orders of magnitude, not a factor of four.

conversation.name: One lock order: the contract row before the lease rows

title: One lock order: the contract row before the lease rows
text:
The real fix for 0084. The mitigation from Tuesday night stays on until this deploys.

Two transactions want the same two things in opposite orders. Admission locks the org's contract row, then reads the org's live leases to count them. Lease renewal locks the lease row, then reads the contract row to check the org is still under its limit. Before ADR-0025 renewal did not read the contract at all, which is why this is nine weeks old and not nine months old.

Postgres kills one side in a second, so a single deadlock is nothing. What took us down is that renewal retried without a budget: the lease expires, the job is reclaimed, admission re-runs, and the two paths go back into the same cycle. It is a livelock built out of correctly handled deadlocks.

This branch makes both paths take the contract row first, caps renewal retries at five, and adds a test that fails if either path changes its order.

text:
docs/guides/test-sharding.mdx. This is the design Marin asked for. It is not an ADR yet - the number comes when the shape stops moving.

Three options, with numbers from six real suites. One: split by file count, which is what we do. Two: split by the duration of the last green run, longest file into the emptiest shard. Three: split by a rolling average of the last five green runs.

Two is within 4% of an ideal split on all six suites and is one line of arithmetic. Three is better on one suite and worse on two.

Open questions: what happens to a file that has never run, and whether the plan has to be stable between runs. I have written what I think and I do not have evidence for either.

text:
--watch uses LISTEN/NOTIFY through the api's websocket today. Behind a transaction pool there is no session to listen on, so the websocket connects and then never says anything, which is worse than failing.

This detects that and polls instead. Two seconds while a build is queued, backing off to fifteen once it is running.
